cards.title: 1 · Market structures
body: Microeconomics looks at one product, one firm, one household — not the whole nation’s GDP.
**Perfect competition** (the textbook’s starting model) needs all of these at once:

cards.title: Many buyers & sellers
body: Nobody is big enough to set the price. Firm is a *price taker*. Its demand curve is a flat line at market P.

cards.title: Homogeneous product
body: Bags of the same grain look alike. No brand loyalty trick.

cards.title: Perfect information
body: Everyone knows the going price. Raise yours and you sell zero.

cards.title: Free entry / exit + mobility
body: Labour and capital can leave a dying use and enter a fat one. No licence wall.

cards.title: Mnemonic — H.I.M.E.
body: *Homogeneous, Information, Many firms, Entry free.* Drop any letter and the market is already “imperfect”.

cards.title: Market
body: **Imperfect markets** (for contrast): monopoly (one seller), oligopoly (few), monopolistic competition (many but branded). Price makers face a downward-sloping demand curve.

cards.title: Left: market sets P. Right: one tiny firm can sell all it wants at that P — horizontal demand.
1.1.1 Market Structure
body: Markets are structured or built up of buyers on one side and sellers on the other side.
The behavior of a seller is influenced by the features (structure) of the market in which he/she sells his/her products and the costs of production.
The major organizational features of markets are called the structure of a market or market structure.
Entry can vary from perfectly free or no barrier to totally blocked or no entry.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All of the following are characteristics of a monopoly except:

options.A: A product which has no close substitutes

cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the characteristics of a monopoly**
A monopoly is defined by a single seller, a unique product with no close substitutes, and extremely high barriers to entry.

**Step 2: Identify the incorrect characteristic**
Free entry to the market is a characteristic of perfect competition and monopolistic competition. In a monopoly, entry is blocked or highly restricted.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, **Free entry to the market** is not a characteristic of a monopoly.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The demand curve facing a monopolist is:

options.C: Downward sloping from left to right
options.D: Upward sloping from left to right

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the relation between monopolist and market**
A monopolist is the sole supplier of the product in the entire market. Therefore, the demand curve facing the monopolist is the market demand curve itself.

**Step 2: Define market demand shape**
Since consumers buy more at lower prices and less at higher prices, the market demand curve slopes downward from left to right.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The monopolist faces a demand curve that is **Downward sloping from left to right**.

cards.title: Demand and supply
body: **Demand:** quantities buyers will take at each price, other things equal. Law: P up → Qd down (usually).
**Supply:** quantities sellers will offer. Law: P up → Qs up.
Move *along* the curve when the good’s own price changes. *Shift* the whole curve when income, tastes, input costs, weather, number of firms, expected future prices change.

cards.title: Trick
body: Price of the good itself = slide on the line. Everything else = new line. Examiners live on that distinction.

cards.problem: Market for sorghum. Drought kills half the crop. What happens to the supply curve and to P?

steps.text: Drought is not “the price of sorghum” — it is a shifter (worse conditions).
Supply shifts left (less offered at every price).
Demand unchanged → new meeting point: higher P, lower Q.

cards.answer: Demand unchanged → new meeting point: higher P, lower Q.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Equilibrium Price and Quantity
body: The interaction of demand and supply determines the equilibrium market price and equilibrium quantity of any good or service.
Equilibrium Price: Equilibrium price is the market price where the quantity demanded for a good or service is exactly equal to the quantity of the good or service supplied.
The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity of the good or service that buyers want to buy and the quantity sellers want to sell is the same.
The equilibrium market price is Pe, while the equilibrium quantity is Qe.

cards.title: 1.3.1 Elasticity of Demand
body: For some goods and services, a small change in the price affects quantity demanded greatly.
For others, a small change in the price has no appreciable effect on the quantity demanded.
Price elasticity of demand thus measures responsiveness of buyers to the change in the price of the good or service under consideration.
Price elasticity of demand is thus a unitfree measure that is conventionally expressed in terms of positive or absolute value.

cards.title: 1.3.2 Elasticity of Supply
body: Elasticity of supply is the measure of the degree to which quantity supplied responds to changes in one of the variables which affect the quantity supplied.
The interpretation is that an increase in the price of sun eyeglasses by 10 per cent will lead to the increase in the quantity of eyeglasses supplied by 30 per cent.
When price increases from Nakfa 2,000 to Nakfa, 3,000 the percentage change in quantity of maize supplied = (700-400/400) x100 = +75%.
The interpretation is that an increase in the price of maize by10 per cent will increase quantity of maize supplied by 15 per cent.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: An oligopolistic market is characterized by:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define oligopoly**
The prefix 'oligo' means few. An oligopoly is a market structure dominated by a small number of large firms.

**Step 2: Analyze key features**
Because of the small number of sellers, these firms exhibit mutual interdependence, where the actions of one directly affect the others.

**Step 3: Final Result**
An oligopolistic market is characterized by **A few sellers**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the price of milk increases, other things being equal, the law of demand states that:

options.B: The quantity of milk demanded will decrease
options.C: The demand for tea will decrease
options.D: The supply of milk will decrease

cards.why:
**Step 1: State the Law of Demand**
The Law of Demand states that price and quantity demanded have an inverse relationship, meaning an increase in price leads to a decrease in the quantity demanded.

**Step 2: Distinguish demand from quantity demanded**
A change in the product's own price causes a change in quantity demanded (a movement along the curve), not a change in demand itself (a shift of the curve).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, **The quantity of milk demanded will decrease**.

cards.title: 1.4 Cost of Production
body: The word ‘Cost’ is commonly used in day to day life and is at the centre of many economic decisions made at the individual, household, firm, national and international level.
Accountants tend to be more concerned with the firm’s finances because they have to keep track of assets and liabilities and evaluate the financial performance.
Economic cost is somewhat different from accounting cost and it is related to the opportunity cost concept.
Although opportunity cost is often hidden, it should be taken into account when making decisions.
Sunk cost is an expenditure that has been made and that cannot be recovered.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the price of commodity 'A' rises and the quantity demanded for commodity 'B' increases, then these commodities must be:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define substitute goods**
Substitutes are goods that can be used in place of one another. When the price of good A increases, consumers switch to the relatively cheaper good B.

**Step 2: Analyze the movement**
An increase in the price of A leads to an increase in the demand (and quantity demanded) of B. This positive cross-price relationship represents substitutes.

**Step 3: Final Result**
These commodities must be **Substitutes**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: For which of the following products does weather have the greatest influence on its supply?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Evaluate factors affecting supply**
Weather is an uncontrollable natural determinant of supply. Favorable weather causes bumper harvests; droughts or frost destroy crops.

**Step 2: Identify the agricultural link**
While factories can control their indoor manufacturing environments, crops and livestock are directly exposed to and dependent on atmospheric weather.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, weather has the greatest influence on **Agricultural products**.

cards.title: 1.5 Consumer Choice and Demand
body: In general, all individuals face two facts of economic life when they make their choices on consumption of goods and services.
Preferences do not represent actual choices.
In explaining consumer preferences, economists make certain assumptions.

The first assumption is that consumers are able to compare one bundle of goods to other bundle of goods and state either they prefer one to the other or be entirely indifferent between the alternatives.
Other important assumption is that individuals are rational in making decisions and they prefer more than less of the goods and services they consume.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Price elasticity of demand measures the percentage change in quantity demanded for a 1 percent change in:
cards.why:
**Step 1: State the definition of Price Elasticity of Demand (Ped)**
Ped measures how responsive consumers are to price changes. It is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

**Step 2: Interpret the 1 percent concept**
Thus, it yields the percentage change in quantity demanded in response to a 1 percent change in the price of the good itself.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The answer is **The price of a good**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If a 10 percent decrease in the price of a good results in a 30 percent increase in the quantity demanded, the price elasticity of demand is:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the Ped formula**
$$\text{Ped} = \frac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P}$$

**Step 2: Substitute the given values**
$$\%\Delta Q = 30\%$$
$$\%\Delta P = -10\%$$
$$\text{Ped} = \frac{30\%}{|-10\%|} = 3$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
The price elasticity of demand is **3**.

glossary.meaning: Monopoly (one seller), oligopoly (few), monopolistic competition (many but branded).
A market is an institution or a mechanism, through which sellers and buyers interact and engage in the exchange of their goods, services and resources (inputs).
Oligopoly is a market structure where there are a few sellers that produce homogeneous or heterogeneous products.
Compared to a perfect competition, oligopoly is an inefficient market as buyers are charged higher prices.
Each seller has a certain degree of monopoly as it is the only producer of the particular brand or variety of the products.
Monopolistic competition is a market condition in which large numbers of firms (sellers) produce similar but differentiated products.
Oligopoly is a market structure where there are a few sellers that produce homogeneous or heterogeneous products.
Duopoly is a market structure where there are only two sellers of homogenous or differentiated products.
Imperfect competition occurs when there are a number of competing sellers (firms) but the market lacks some or all the features of perfect competition.
Interdependence refers to the degree to which the actions of one firm affect the actions of the others.
Demand is the amount of goods or services consumers are willing and able to purchase at a given price and at a given time.
Perfect market is a theoretical market structure in which there are many buyers and sellers of homogenous products where no single seller or buyer has the power to influence the market price.
Individual demand is the quantity of goods or services demanded by an individual buyer (consumer) at a given price and time.
Market demand is the aggregate or the total amount of quantity demanded by all buyers (consumers).
Demand schedule is a table showing the relationship between the price of a good or service and the quantity of the good or service demanded in a given period of time, other things being equal.
Demand curve is a diagram showing the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded in a given period of time, other things being equal.
Market price is the main determinant of the quantity demanded for goods and services by consumers.
Supply curve is a curve or a graph that shows the amount of goods or services sold/offered at different prices.

tips.text: In a free market, economic decisions are coordinated by market mechanism.
The operation of the market system allows resources to be allocated, and goods and services to be produced and distributed in accordance with the market forces of demand and supply.
Economic decisions have to be made both by consumers and by producers.
Consumers can choose between a large number of goods and services supplied into the market.
For each good, consumers must decide how much they are willing and able to buy from the market.
Producers must decide how much they are going to produce and supply into the market.
Consumers and producers meet each other in the market.
Coordination between the total quantity demanded by consumers and the total quantity supplied by producers is achieved through the interaction of the market supply and demand.
Economists group different market structures into five categories. These categories are perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and duopoly.
With the exception of perfect competition, all the other market structures are collectively referred to imperfect markets.
Many buyers & sellers: Nobody is big enough to set the price. Firm is a price taker. Its demand curve is a flat line at market P.
Homogeneous product: Bags of the same grain look alike. No brand loyalty trick.
Perfect information: Everyone knows the going price. Raise yours and you sell zero.
Free entry / exit + mobility: Labour and capital can leave a dying use and enter a fat one. No licence wall.

similar.q: Ranking the market structure from most competitive to least competitive, we have  A) monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition, perfect competition.  B) perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly.  C) oligopoly, monopoly, monopolistic competition, perfect competition.  D) perfect competition, oligopoly, monopolistic competition, monopoly.  E) perfect competition, monopolistic competition, monopoly, oligopoly.
similar.a: B. perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly. — A is the reverse order. Answer: B.
